strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing an underexplored dimension of MoE—adapting expert capacity rather than just expert selection
Simple and practical approach integrating naturally into standard MoE pipelines with minimal modifications via two-width training
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across model scales (55M–1B), routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4), and training budgets with proper ablation studies
Consistent Pareto improvements of 20–36% FLOP reduction at comparable accuracy across all tested configurations, suggesting robust method
Insightful analysis including learned γ patterns (Figure 11), FLOP breakdown (Figure 12), and stable training dynamics (Figure 13)
Lightweight test-time training mechanism requiring only 50 calibration batches with frozen model parameters
Clear presentation with well-organized methodology and informative visualizations of compute-quality trade-offs
weaknesses: Critical limitation to small-scale models (up to 1B parameters)—no experiments on 7B–70B scale models standard in 2026, raising serious questions about practical relevance and scalability

Cannot be applied to existing pre-trained models; requires multi-width training from scratch, eliminating applicability to current large language models that practitioners fine-tune rather than retrain
No comparison to alternative efficient inference methods (quantization, pruning, distillation, speculative decoding), making it unclear how MoSE performs relative to standard efficiency techniques
Training overhead not quantified—paper claims 'low overhead' from two-width training but provides no concrete wall-clock time or training cost comparison
Actual latency and hardware efficiency not reported; uses only MFLOPs per token metric without demonstrating that FLOP reductions translate to actual speedups
Test-time training details underexplored: only 50 batches for calibration without sensitivity analysis; SGD learning rate 0.01 choice unexplained; no convergence curves shown
Width configuration choices (discrete set {0.25, 0.30, ..., 1.00} with step 0.05) not justified; no ablation on discretization strategy or continuous width alternatives
Limited downstream task evaluation with only 2 small benchmarks (LAMBADA with 5153 and WSC with 273 examples); no evaluation on diverse or larger-scale downstream tasks
Budget parameter Γ in Equation 10 inadequately explained—unclear how to specify it in practice or how sensitive results are to its choices
Unclear generalization of learned γ across domains; transfer tested only on closely related language modeling tasks, not on truly different domains or modalities

strengths: Clear motivation and simple approach: identifies that MoE models execute full-width experts despite sparse selection, and proposes parameter-slicing as a straightforward solution

Comprehensive experimental evaluation within scope: multiple model scales (55M-1B), routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4), training budgets (3B-15B tokens), and evaluation datasets (OpenWebText, WikiText-103, LAMBADA, WSC)
Stable training recipe: two-width sampling strategy is practical, requires no MoE pipeline modifications, and demonstrably maintains training stability (Figure 3)
Consistent empirical improvements: achieves better compute-quality Pareto frontiers than standard MoE across most evaluated settings
Well-documented experimental details: hyperparameters, architectures, evaluation protocols, and compute methodology support reproducibility
Multiple inference strategies explored: uniform, router-conditioned, and test-time training modes with thoughtful ablation (Figure 10)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward application of well-established slimmable networks (Yu et al. 2019; Kusupati et al. 2022) to MoE experts; test-time training is minimal (scalar γ per layer); feels incremental rather than a novel conceptual contribution

Critical scale limitation: all experiments on ≤1B parameter models; modern MoE deployed at 100B+ parameters; authors explicitly acknowledge inability to apply post-training and uncertainty about scaling; major practical applicability concern

Missing comparison with related work: recent elastic MoE methods (RoE, EMoE) mentioned but never compared empirically; unclear how MoSE differs from or outperforms these approaches; no comparison with other efficient MoE variants

Weak justification for width allocation: mapping from router probabilities to widths (Eqs. 7-10) lacks principled motivation; why should expert-selection probability correlate with optimal execution width? Simple normalized-probability baseline (γ=1.0) suggests limited sophistication

Unexplained generalization: uniform-width training is asserted to generalize to non-uniform inference-time allocation, but no analysis provided; why learned representations should work across diverse width configurations is unclear

Missing critical analyses: no per-expert or per-token width analysis; no exploration of which inputs/experts benefit from narrower widths; no ablation on training design choices (why two widths? why uniform sampling?); no analysis of effects on model coherence

Modest improvements without statistical validation: many results show 1-2 PPL improvements (e.g., Table 1) with no confidence intervals or significance testing; with limited runs, improvements may be within noise margins

Lack of practical performance metrics: no wall-clock time or latency measurements; FLOPs reduction doesn't guarantee speedup without hardware-specific analysis; no memory overhead quantification; no batching efficiency analysis
Cannot adapt existing models: requires training from scratch with slimmable structure from inception; cannot be applied to pre-trained models, limiting real-world utility

Incomplete downstream evaluation: mostly language modeling tasks; LAMBADA (5153 ex.) and WSC (273 ex.) are small benchmarks; no instruction-following, reasoning, or other critical LLM capabilities evaluated; results may not transfer to fine-tuned or specialized models
Experimental confounds: MoSE (w=1.0) sometimes outperforms standard MoE baseline despite identical full-width execution (Table 1), suggesting potential confounding factors not explained

Test-time training limitations: requires calibration set (50 batches); Figure 9 shows mixed transfer to LAMBADA with 'mild non-monotonicity'; claimed negligible overhead but no timing provided; practical applicability questionable

Underdeveloped ablations: no comparison with simply increasing activated experts; no exploration of alternative width sampling strategies; no investigation of router entropy or uncertainty-based width allocation as alternatives to probability-based mapping

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach combining slimmable networks with MoE to enable variable-width expert execution, addressing a previously unexplored dimension of conditional computation in MoE architectures
Simple and practical training recipe requiring only two-width sampling per iteration with no modifications to standard MoE pipeline, ensuring easy adoption

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model scales (55M-1B), routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4), and training budgets (3B-15B tokens) with consistent improvements (17.4%-35.9% FLOP reductions)

Strong empirical results with full-width MoSE matching/improving baseline MoE and TTT consistently shifting Pareto frontier; improvements stable across model scales and generalize to different routing configurations

Thorough ablation studies and analysis including training stability (Figure 3), inference mode isolation (Figure 10), learned parameter interpretability (Figure 11), FLOPs breakdown justifying effectiveness (Figure 12), and width-wise convergence analysis (Figure 13)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, optimization settings, training schedules, and calibration procedures fully specified in appendices enabling reliable reproduction
Clear presentation and well-motivated writing with effective visualizations communicating core ideas; honest discussion of limitations without overclaiming
weaknesses: Experiments limited to small-scale GPT-2 models (55M-1B parameters); applicability to modern large-scale LLMs (70B+) remains unclear, raising fundamental questions about scalability of multi-width training at scale
Slimmable capability must be incorporated during training and cannot be applied to existing pretrained models without retraining, significantly limiting practical applicability and adoption
Missing empirical comparisons with recent related work (Elastic MoE, RoE) discussed conceptually but not evaluated—comparison only against standard MoE weakens positioning
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple-run statistics reported; uncertain whether perplexity differences at similar compute budgets are statistically significant
Limited analysis of test-time training γ calibration: minimal exploration of data sensitivity, only single domain transfer example (LAMBADA), unclear robustness under significant distribution shift
Incomplete technical analysis of why learning γ dramatically outperforms fixed γ=1.0; missing investigation of expert specialization patterns with different widths and router behavior adaptation

Paper focuses exclusively on FLOPs; actual wall-clock latency and practical hardware utilization effects not analyzed, undermining practical deployment conclusions as variable-width execution may not achieve linear FLOP-latency correspondence
Discrete width set design choice (0.05 step size) not justified; no ablation or sensitivity analysis of discretization strategy or exploration of continuous width alternatives
Technical details on gradient flow and potential training instabilities under multi-width training not thoroughly discussed; unclear gradient handling through different width paths

strengths: Addresses a genuine problem: MoE models exhibit discontinuous accuracy-compute tradeoffs, and MoSE enables smooth inference-time spectrum

Consistent inference-time improvements: 20-40% FLOPs reduction at matched perplexity across diverse model scales (55M-2.5B), routing configurations (E8A2, E8A4, E16A4, E64A8, E128A8), and evaluation benchmarks

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple datasets (OpenWebText, WikiText-103, LAMBADA, WSC, HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA), thorough ablations (Figure 8 comparing inference modes, Figure 13 γ visualization), and systematic scaling studies (Figures 4-6)

Extensive diagnostics and reproducibility support: routing stability analysis (Appendix B.5) confirms no expert collapse, runtime validation (Appendix B.4) shows FLOPs-latency correlation, width-wise training dynamics (Figure 15) demonstrate stable convergence

Practical deployment pathway: post-hoc adaptation via continual pretraining (CPT) enables adding slimmability to existing MoE checkpoints (demonstrated on DeepSeek-V2-Lite), with modest overhead achieving meaningful gains

Technical soundness: simple multi-width training approach integrates cleanly into standard MoE pipeline without architectural modifications; test-time training learns only one scalar (or layer-wise) parameter, minimizing calibration cost

Clear presentation: well-organized paper with effective visualization of Pareto frontiers, detailed hyperparameters (Appendix A), and thoughtful impact statement addressing safety across execution widths
Zero-shot transfer validated: improvements generalize to downstream reasoning tasks (HellaSwag, PIQA, SIQA) and across datasets (LAMBADA transfer in Figure 9), not just pretraining perplexity
weaknesses: Scale limitations: largest from-scratch trained model is 2.5B parameters with 50B tokens, not frontier scale; acknowledged limitation 'we do not yet report full from-scratch training at frontier MoE scale' reduces impact assessment

Claimed advantage at full width not uniformly supported: Table 1 shows GPT2-Small 15B regresses (31.03→31.26) and GPT2-Standard 3B shows marginal gain (27.75→27.66); abstract claim 'matches or improves standard MoE at full width' overstates evidence
Incremental contribution: combining two existing ideas (slimmable networks + MoE) in straightforward fashion; novelty is more in engineering than algorithmic innovation

Generalization assumption lacks justification: paper claims 'learned representations generalize well to non-uniform, router-conditioned allocations' despite training only on uniform widths, but provides no theoretical or deep empirical analysis of why this holds

Test-time training design underexplored: uses only 50 batches for γ calibration without sensitivity analysis; Figure 9 shows dataset transfer but not budget transfer (how does γ learned for Γ₁ perform on Γ₂?)
Missing empirical baselines: no direct comparison to related elastic MoE methods (RoE, EMoE) mentioned in related work; comparison is qualitative only
Width discretization choice unmotivated: step size 0.05 for width set A has no justification or ablation study
Inference-time complexity not fully characterized: claims TTT is 'lightweight' but adds optimization step; actual calibration cost (time/compute) not quantified relative to inference
Code availability issue: manuscript references 'The code can be found at:' but URL is blank/missing, hindering reproducibility
Limited architecture scope: width adaptation targets only FFN layers; attention computation unchanged, so improvements capped by expert contribution to total FLOPs

strengths: Comprehensive systematic evaluation across multiple model scales (55M-2.5B+), routing configurations, and pre-training budgets with consistent 20-40% FLOP improvements
Solid empirical results with good ablation studies (inference modes, training dynamics, routing diagnostics, transferability)
Practical method applicable to existing pretrained MoE models via continual pre-training
Clear presentation with informative figures and extensive appendix
Lightweight test-time training (TTT) mechanism that effectively learns width allocation without modifying model parameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (slimmable networks, multi-width training) without significant methodological innovation
Key design choice under-analyzed: why representations trained with uniform widths generalize well to non-uniform, router-conditioned inference lacks mechanistic explanation
Missing critical comparisons: no direct evaluation against related methods (Elastic MoE, RoE) or simpler baselines (varying k, pruning, quantization)
Limited experimental scale: largest from-scratch model is 2.5B parameters; only one large-scale continual pre-training experiment; results on frontier-scale MoE models (≥10B) absent
Insufficient training cost analysis: claimed 'low overhead' but no detailed timing measurements, wall-clock comparisons, or continual pre-training cost quantification provided
Test-time training calibration uses only 50 batches (300 examples); sensitivity to calibration set size and distribution shift unexplored
Width selection mechanism (Equations 7-10) appears ad-hoc: normalized probability raised to power γ lacks principled justification; alternative formulations not explored
No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing; results appear to be single runs
Code availability compromised: URL incomplete ('The code can be found at: .')
Shallow analysis of learned representations: which experts/tokens benefit from width reduction; what patterns emerge in width allocation decisions

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model scales (55M-2.5B), routing configurations (E8A2 through E128A8), and pre-training budgets (3B-50B tokens), demonstrating consistent improvements in compute-quality Pareto frontiers (17-41% FLOPs reduction)
Clean, practical methodology: simple two-width training (Eq. 6) adds minimal overhead; lightweight test-time training optimizes only low-dimensional parameter γ with 50 batches and no weight updates

Thorough analysis addressing key concerns: routing diagnostics (Figs 17-19) show no expert imbalance; ablation (Fig 8) isolates inference mode contributions; γ transferability (Fig 9) demonstrates generalization across datasets

Consistent improvements across diverse settings: zero-shot transfer tasks, multiple model scales, different routing configurations, and continual pretraining on DeepSeek-V2-Lite all show meaningful gains
Well-motivated contribution: the observation that MoE leaves expert capacity unexploited is clear, and using routing probabilities as signals for width allocation is elegant and well-justified
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters (Table 3), extensive diagnostics in appendix, width-wise dynamics analysis, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily combines two well-established techniques (slimmable networks from Yu et al. 2019, Rippel et al. 2014; random-width training from Tastan et al. 2025, Horvath et al. 2021). Test-time training (Eq. 12) reduces to SGD on a scalar parameter, which is straightforward rather than innovative

Critical frontier-scale validation gap: full pretraining maxes out at GPT2-Large (2.5B/50B tokens); DeepSeek-V2-Lite (16B) only evaluated via continual pretraining, not from-scratch. Modern MoE systems operate 10-100× larger—without demonstrating benefits at frontier scale, practical impact is unclear

No empirical comparison to related efficiency approaches: RoE (Zibakhsh et al. 2025) and EMoE (Gu et al. 2025) are mentioned but not compared experimentally. Cannot assess whether MoSE is superior or complementary, limiting contextualization

Design choices lack sufficient justification: (1) Why optimize γ specifically rather than per-expert or per-token width multipliers? (2) Router signal quality assumption (routing probabilities indicate importance) is underexplored—robustness to poor routing is not discussed. (3) Width discretization granularity (step 0.05) impact is not studied

Hardware realism concerns: FLOPs↔latency correlation (Fig 16) shown for one setting; partial expert execution may suffer from irregular memory access and poor cache behavior not addressed. Real-world speedups could be smaller than FLOPs suggest

No comparison to alternative baselines: missing comparisons to expert pruning, adaptive routing, or simply using top-2k routing with full-width experts. Unclear how gains compare to other MoE efficiency techniques
Statistical rigor gaps: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; single-run results raise uncertainty about variance; smaller differences lack significance testing
Limited architectural scope: only FFN intermediate dimension is slimmable. Generalizability to other components (attention, embeddings) or other architectures (encoder-decoder, vision) is unexplored

Routing signal assumptions underexplored: why should reduced-width performance correlate with routing probability? No analysis of when width adaptation helps/hurts, failure cases, or routing entropy correlation with compute value

Key claim underspecified: the assertion that 'learned representations generalize well to non-uniform, router-conditioned allocations' (page 3) despite training with uniform widths lacks detailed justification or analysis
